title: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 141. Scope: digit sequences of higher roots, logarithms and exponentials of small integers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large finite samples of these constants are easy to compute and test. The claim lacks a defined measure for almost all and ranges over infinite families, preventing full resolution from existing computation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define distributions over small integer inputs and function classes, compute long digit expansions in specified bases, and apply fixed randomness tests. Estimate the fraction passing each test and identify systematic counterfamilies.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite tests cannot establish asymptotic randomness.

Almost all requires a measure over numbers and operations.

Known special identities can create selected regular cases.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.6
data existence: 0.92
analysis feasibility: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The constants Wolfram lists are all computable to high precision with standard libraries, so the appearance claim is testable on a wide explicit range. 'Almost all' is a quantitative hedge that a sample can estimate only after the range is chosen, and a few structured exceptions are easy to produce by choice of base. The computation therefore settles a specified sample, which is part of the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute long digit prefixes of cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms, and exponentials of small integers and score them with the same randomness tests used for square roots. A recurring pattern in a declared 'simple' family would challenge 'almost all'; uniform irregularity would support the claim inside that family.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Almost all' and 'simple numbers' need an explicit finite range before a failure rate means anything.

Special cases with known structure, such as logarithms of powers of the base, have to be excluded or they trivially fail randomness.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.65
